conversation.content: Actually, leaning too hard into split complementary schemes can backfire—sometimes the “balance” you’re chasing ends up feeling forced or sterile, especially if it ignores the emotional tone your brand actually needs. content.text: By relying on memorization, existing language models are unable to generate factually correct text about real-world entities. In particular, they are unable to capture the long tail of rare entities and word types like numbers and dates. In this work, we proposed the  knowledge graph language model (KGLM), a neural language model that can access an external source of facts, encoded as a knowledge graph, in order to generate text. Our implementa- tion is available at:  https://github.com/rloganiv/ kglm-model . We also introduced  Linked WikiText- 2  containing text that has been aligned to facts in the knowledge graph, allowing efﬁcient training of the model.  Linked WikiText-2  is freely avail- able for download at:  https://rloganiv.github.io/ linked-wikitext-2 . In our evaluation, we showed that by utilizing this graph, the proposed KGLM is able to generate higher-quality, factually correct text that includes mentions of rare entities and spe- ciﬁc tokens like numbers and dates.

Table  4  presents performance of each language model on the relations. The  oracle  KGLM is given the correct entity annotation for    $X$  , while the  NEL KGLM uses the discriminative model used for im- portance sampling combined with the NEL entity linker to produce an entity annotation for    $X$  .

overestimates the probability of out-of-vocabulary tokens when they are mapped to a single UNK token. This is problematic for comparing the per- formance of the KGLM to traditional language models on  Linked WikiText-2  since there are a large number of rare entities whose alias tokens are out- of-vocabulary. That is, even if the KGLM identiﬁes the correct entity and copies the correct alias token with high probability, other models can attain bet- ter perplexity by assigning a higher probability to UNK. Accordingly, we also measure  unknown pe- nalized perplexity  (UPP) (a.k.a  adjusted perplexity ) introduced by  Ueberla  ( 1994 ), and used recently by  Ahn et al.  ( 2016 ) and  Spithourakis and Riedel ( 2018 ). This metric penalizes the probability of UNK tokens by evenly dividing their probability mass over  $\mathcal{U}$  , the set of tokens that get mapped to UNK . We can be compute UPP by replacing  $p(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{K})$   in the perplexity above by  $\textstyle{\frac{1}{|{\mathcal{U}}|}}p(\mathbf{U}\mathbf{N}\mathbf{K})$  , where    $|\mathcal{U}|$   is estimated from the data.

- AWD-LSTM: PPL = 74.8, UPP = 165.8
- KGLM*: PPL = 44.1 (bold), UPP = 88.5 (bold)

The lowest values in each column (KGLM*) are bolded, indicating superior performance. The table is bordered at the top and bottom with thick horizontal lines, and there is a thinner line separating the header from the data rows. The layout is clean, with model names left-aligned and metric values right-aligned.

If your message needs urgency, rebellion, or chaos, forcing harmony might actually dull your voice instead of amplifying it. I’ve seen brands swap textbook triads for clashing analogous combos—like neon orange against deep navy—and watch engagement skyrocket because the palette matched their attitude, not a rulebook. Balance is great for calm, but real impact lives in tension, and sometimes the “wrong” palette gets more clicks than the “right” one. Test it: throw a jarring combo at your audience and see which one sticks in their minds. Memorability beats symmetry every time—if they remember how you made them feel, you’ve already won.

conversation.content: Responsible infographic design isn’t just about looking good—it’s about being clear, credible, and accessible. High contrast ensures legibility for all viewers, especially those with visual impairments, while thoughtful typography keeps the message digestible even at a glance. Source citations aren’t an afterthought; they build trust and let audiences verify claims, turning graphics into tools for informed decisions. Too many infographics prioritize aesthetics over function, but real impact comes from balancing visual appeal with usability. If your data is solid but your design confuses or excludes people, you’ve missed the point. Design with purpose—not just pixels—and make sure every element serves clarity, credibility, and connection.

The image consists of a square grid containing 36 circles arranged in 6 rows and 6 columns. The circles are evenly spaced and all are of equal size. The circles alternate between two styles: filled (solid black) and unfilled (white with a black outline). The pattern follows a checkerboard-like arrangement:

- The first row (topmost) contains only unfilled circles.
- The second row contains only filled circles.
- The third row contains only unfilled circles.
- The fourth row contains only filled circles.
- The fifth row contains only unfilled circles.
- The sixth row (bottommost) contains only filled circles.

The background is white, and the grid is centered within a thin black border. There is no text, chart, or additional graphical elements present. The overall layout is symmetrical and visually balanced.

This image is a historical infographic titled "Carte Figurative des pertes successives en hommes de l’Armée Française dans la campagne de Russie 1812-1813," created by Charles Joseph Minard in 1869. It visually represents the losses suffered by Napoleon’s army during the Russian campaign of 1812-1813.

**Layout and Main Subjects:**
- The map is horizontally oriented, with the French army’s advance (in tan/beige) from the left (west, starting at Kowno) to the right (east, ending at Moscow), and the retreat (in black) from Moscow back to Kowno.
- The width of the colored bands corresponds to the number of soldiers at each stage, with numbers labeled along the route (e.g., 422,000 at Kowno, 100,000 at Moscow, and drastically fewer on the return).
- Major cities and rivers along the route are labeled, including Kowno, Wilna, Smolensk, Moscow, and others.
- The top section contains a detailed handwritten French description explaining the methodology and sources.

**Spatial Relations:**
- The tan band (advance) starts wide at Kowno and narrows as it progresses eastward, indicating decreasing troop numbers.
- The black band (retreat) starts at Moscow and narrows even more rapidly, showing catastrophic losses.
- The route is annotated with city names and troop numbers at various points.
- Vertical lines connect the route to a lower graph.

**Lower Section:**
- Below the main map is a line graph labeled "TABLEAU GRAPHIQUE de la température en degrés du thermomètre de Réaumur au dessous de zéro," showing temperature readings during the retreat, with dates and corresponding temperatures (e.g., -21° on Nov 28, -30° on Dec 6).
- The temperature graph is aligned with the retreat path, visually correlating troop losses with extreme cold.

**Colors and Text:**
- The advance is shown in tan/beige, the retreat in black.
- City names, troop numbers, and temperature values are labeled in black text.
- The title and explanatory text are in ornate French script at the top.
- The map includes a scale for distance in French leagues.

**Charts and Axes:**
- The main chart is a flow map, with band width as the axis for troop numbers.
- The lower chart is a line graph with temperature (Réaumur scale) as the y-axis and dates as the x-axis.

**Summary:**
This image is a classic example of data visualization, showing the catastrophic losses of Napoleon’s army during the Russian campaign, correlating troop numbers, geographic progression, and temperature. It is widely regarded as one of the most effective infographics ever created, combining spatial, quantitative, and temporal data in a single visual narrative.

Real connection comes from vulnerability, not vector overlays. You can tame stock all day, but if your audience can’t smell the humanity behind the pixels, you’re still shouting into a void. The whole family can explore  the world of science and technology at  the  VilVite Science Centre.
